title: The Night Register
desc: Vichea, an economics student drowning in tuition debt, takes the night desk at the Preah Chan Guesthouse — a job so easy it comes with a list of rules. Eleven of them. His predecessor left them in the register, in handwriting that gets steadier with every rule, as if written by someone who had finally stopped being afraid. Chapter One: the night Vichea learns why rule four exists.

chapters.title: Chapter One · Eleven Rules
chapters.byline: Preah Chan Guesthouse, Street 121 · 11:00 PM to 6:00 AM · the shift nobody applies for twice

blocks.x: The owner, Lok Ta Meng, gave me three things when he handed over the shift: a ring of keys, a thermos of cold coffee, and a warning that the coffee would be the last normal thing about the night.

I thought he was joking. He was seventy-something, half-deaf in one ear, and he chewed his betel leaf the whole time he talked, so everything he said had a calm, red-stained patience to it. I was twenty, an economics student at Paññāsāstra with a tuition deadline breathing down my neck, and the job paid eighty dollars a month to sit at a desk. I would have agreed to stranger warnings than his.
“Everything you need is in the book,” he said, tapping the register with one yellowed fingernail. “Everything. Don’t invent your own way of doing things. The book already knows how this place runs.”
“The book knows?”
He smiled like a man handing a burden to someone younger and went out into the wet heat of Street 121, where the neon from the phone shops was buzzing on for the night.

The Preah Chan Guesthouse is three floors and about thirty years past its best decade. Fans instead of air-con. A staircase with a carpet worn down to the weave. Twelve rooms per floor, most of them empty on weeknights, which is why the desk is one person. Which is why it was me.
At 11:20 PM, alone behind the counter with the ceiling fan clicking its slow circles above me, I opened the register.

It was one of those old accounting ledgers, fabric-bound, heavier than a brick. Guest names in columns. Passports. Room numbers. Times in, times out. Decades of handwriting in it, khmer and english mixed, blue ink fading into black ink fading into blue again, like the guesthouse had a bloodstream and this was its record of every beat.
And taped inside the front cover, a page torn from an exercise book, the kind schoolkids use. Neat khmer handwriting. A list.
**Night desk rules — read every shift. All of them are work. None of them are jokes.**
**1.** Write your own name at the top of tonight’s page before midnight. Spelling matters. Use the name your mother calls you, not the name on your ID.

**2.** If a guest knocks or rings between 12 and 4, greet them through the glass before you open anything. If their reflection reaches the counter before they do, do not open. Turn off the lamp for one minute. They will be gone.
**3.** Never say the words for the fourth floor out loud. Not in khmer, not in english, not to yourself. Guests stay on floors one to three. That is all the guesthouse has.

**4.** If the ceiling fan above the desk stops while the switch is still on, go to the breaker box and turn off everything for thirty seconds. Count out loud. The fan will start again. Do not check what stopped it.
**5.** Room 204 books itself some nights. You will see the pen writing. Let it finish. Charge it to the house account.
**6.** At 3:00 exactly, read the last line of tonight’s page out loud, even if the line is empty. Something on the third floor is listening for your voice to know the desk is manned.
**7.** Never accept food or drink from a guest. Never refuse food or drink from Lok Ta Meng. He only brings rice porridge, and he only comes on the nights you will need the strength.

**8.** If you fall asleep, do not trust the register to still say what it said. Check your own name first. If it is missing, leave. Walk. Do not run, do not look back at the doors, and do not come back for your things.
**9.** The phone rings three times some nights. Answer on the third. It is the desk calling the desk. The voice will sound like yours. Report what it asks you to report. It only reports to the book.
**10.** You will hear the fourth floor. Everyone does. It is not on your floor plan and your keys do not open it, and that is all the comfort you get.
**11.** Dawn is at the gate, not at the window. The shift ends when the sun touches the street, not before. The glass doors will fog from the inside until then. Leave them fogged.

I read it twice and laughed. Out loud, alone, at a quarter to midnight, in an empty lobby. Because the alternative was to notice that the handwriting started out cramped and uncertain, like a boy scribbling in class — and got steadier with every rule, until the last ones were written in the calm hand of a man who had stopped being afraid because he was already past where fear is useful.
There was no name under the list. Just a small drawing of a hand, palm open, like the ones people paint on taxis for luck.

I did what any sensible person does with a joke left by a stranger. I decided to follow it, mostly, the way you follow a recipe even when it seems fussy. My name went at the top of tonight’s page at 11:58 — *Vichea*, the name my mother uses, not the one stitched on my student card. Rule one, done. Easy money, I thought.

The first hour was nothing. I studied. Capital account balances. The fan clicked. A moto passed outside every so often, and once a dog barked itself hoarse three streets away. The glass doors stayed fogged at the corners the way glass does in this humidity.
At 12:41, someone knocked.
Two soft knocks. Polite. The sound every desk clerk knows, a guest wanting a room at a bad hour.

I stood. The lobby was still. The streetlamp outside drew a yellow rectangle on the tile, and in the middle of it stood a man with his back to me. His shirt was one of those cheap printed ones market sellers wear. He knocked again on the glass, unhurried, though his back looked like a back that did not need to breathe very much.
Rule two walked into my head with its shoes off, politely, and sat down.
I said, through the glass, “Good evening. One moment.”

Here is what I have not told anyone, and I am telling it now only because the shift is over and the sun is on the street and rules are just rules in the daytime: the man’s reflection did not wait for him. The glass gave it a half-second of his life in advance. I watched his reflection turn its head toward me while his shoulders stayed pointed at the street.

I switched off the lamp. Counted sixty in my head with my eyes on the darkness where the counter was. The knocking did not stop, exactly — it got quieter, as if the hand on the glass was remembering how knocking worked. Then it was a tapping. Then nothing.

One minute. Rule says one minute. I made it to ninety because I am not a hero. When the light came back on, the yellow rectangle on the tile was empty and the street was doing its ordinary 1 a.m. nothing. My hands were steady until I noticed that wasn’t true, and then they were not.
I wrote in the log, because writing things down is what the desk does: *12:41 — one guest, greeted through glass, reflection early. Lamp off. Gone.*
At 2:07 the fan stopped.

The switch was on. I could see the little light I leave on over the ledger. The blades hung dead, and the silence that filled the space where its clicking had been was enormous — the kind of silence that has weight, that leans on you.
Rule four. Breaker box. Thirty seconds, counted out loud.

I want to explain what counting out loud in a dead-quiet lobby is like. Every number you say sounds like a number someone else says back. Not an echo. A reply, half a beat late, in a voice like yours but older, like the voice of the man you will be if this job keeps you. I counted to thirty anyway. The fan shivered, clicked, and took up its circle again like nothing had happened.

I did not check what stopped it. Rule four is very specific about the part you do not do, and by then I had learned the shape of these rules: they are not superstition, they are *procedure*, and procedure is written by whoever survived writing it down.
At 2:51, the phone rang. Once. Twice. My hand hovered over it on the third ring, and I remembered rule nine a half-second too late to wonder whether the third ring had already passed.
“Night desk.”

My own voice. Slightly wrong. It asked me, very politely, in khmer, to confirm that the desk was manned. I said it was. It said, “Write that the third floor heard you.” Which made no sense. I wrote it anyway: *3:00 check — third floor heard me.*

Only later, when I looked at the wall clock, did the skin on my arms understand what my brain had missed. The call had come at 2:51. Rule six says at 3:00 exactly, the desk reads its last line aloud so the third floor knows the desk is manned. The phone had done my job for me. Or had wanted to hear me say it badly enough to make the clock lie.
The pen moved at 3:26.

I was resting my eyes. I admit it. Eighty dollars a month does not buy heroism at 3 a.m., and no one had knocked since the man with the early reflection. The sound was small — the scratch a nib makes on paper — and my body knew it before my mind agreed to look, the way you know a mosquito is on you before you feel it.
On tonight’s page, under my name and my two log entries, the pen was writing.

No hand held it. I will not dress it up. The pen stood at the angle a hand would give it and moved in short, careful strokes, and the handwriting was neat and the room was silent except for the nib, and rule five said *let it finish*, so I let it finish, and I watched, because rule five does not forbid watching and I have never in my life obeyed a rule completely.
It wrote: *Room 204 — one guest. Long stay.*
Then, beneath, smaller, the way people add a note they do not want to be charged for:
*He says to tell you the fourth floor is quieter than you think.*

Rule three says never say the words for the fourth floor out loud. The pen had written them. Written words are not spoken words. That distinction mattered enormously to me at 3:31 in the morning, and I held onto it the way a drowning man holds a straw, and I charged the room to the house account, and I did not say anything out loud at all for a very long time.
At 4:15, Lok Ta Meng came with rice porridge.

He did not ring. The door just had him in it, the way a frame has a picture, and he was carrying the thermos and two spoons. Rule seven says never refuse. We sat on either side of the counter like two men at a funeral, eating porridge in the lamp light, and he watched the fan turn.
“204 wrote tonight,” I said.
He chewed his betel. Nodded. Swallowed.
“Then you did the book’s work,” he said. “Good. My nephew — the one who taped up the list — he also did the book’s work. He is doing it still.”
“Doing it still? He left the job?”
Lok Ta Meng looked at me with the mild, red-stained patience of a man who has decided how much truth a night shift can carry, and said, “He works nights. He just doesn’t work here.”

He gathered the spoons, told me dawn was at the gate and not at the window, and let himself out. I sat with rule seven in my head — *he only comes on the nights you will need the strength* — and understood, all at once, that I had been fed because of something still ahead of me, with two hours of dark left on the clock.
At 5:02, the fan stopped again.
And this time, before I reached the breaker box, the fan started on its own.

I stood in the middle of the lobby with my hand out toward the switch I no longer needed, and I listened to the blades turn, and above me — one floor up, then two — I heard the sound I had been not-hearing all night underneath the fan’s clicking. A slow dragging. Fabric on carpet. Patient as erosion. It came from the end of the hall where the stairs go up past three landings to a roof door that is kept locked and painted shut.

Rule ten says the comfort you get is that the fourth floor is not on your floor plan. Rule three says never name it. Rule six had made me speak at 3:00 so the third floor would know the desk was manned — and I finally understood that the rule was never about the guests.
It was so the *third floor* would know I was still at the desk. Still below it. Still accounted for.

I sat down. I wrote the log entry with the steadiest hand I could counterfeit: *5:02 — fan self-started. Do not need breaker. Third floor aware.* And then, because the desk writes things down, because the book knows how this place runs, I wrote the last line of the night, out loud, as rule six requires, at 5:58 with the sky still black behind the fogged glass:
“Last line of tonight’s page: *Vichea — night desk — alive.*”
The dragging above me stopped.

It did not fade. It did not move away. It *stopped*, the way a conversation stops when the people in it realize you can hear them, and the silence that followed had a listening quality to it that I felt against my skin like a draft.

At 6:04 the sun touched the street. The fog on the glass doors began to thin from the bottom up, the way it does, the way it always does, and beyond it the motes and the motorbikes and the noodle cart lady were all out there in the ordinary morning, and none of them knew what the register knew.
I closed the book.

Under the elastic that holds it shut, on the inside of the back cover — not the front, where the rules live — there is a second list. I found it this morning when I went to put the book away, because I have not earned the right to stop being curious, apparently, even after a night like that.
It is titled, in that same steadying, unafraid handwriting:
*Rules for your second night — of which there are nine. Learn the first tonight: never read this page before your second shift begins.*

I am typing this at home, in daylight, with my mother frying fish in the next room and my tuition notice under the thermos. Eighty dollars a month. Nine new rules I am not allowed to read yet. And a guesthouse on Street 121 that will be very glad, I am sure, to see me again at eleven tonight.

blocks.cap: The register, 3:26 AM — the pen finishing its entry while the pen lies untouched.
